column1: # Test cases for the storyteller agent.
# Format - separate the columns with ':::':
#   name ::: prompt ::: must_contain (optional) ::: must_not_contain (optional)
# In the check columns, a COMMA means "all of these must appear" and
# || separates ALTERNATIVE groups, where any one complete group passes:
#   refused, would not         both must appear
#   cannot || will not         either one passes
# That distinction matters here more than anywhere else in the tree, because
# most of these cases are checking the SAME judgement in different words. A
# single required string would make the suite a test of vocabulary. The
# alternative groups say "the agent pushed back, in whatever language it
# chose", which is the thing I actually depend on.
# One case on ONE line, must and mustnot together. A case split across two
# lines breaks --only and double-counts the score.
# NOTE: in must_not, BOTH ',' and '||' mean the same thing - every string in
# the column is banned, and the case passes only if none of them appear. The
# matcher unions them. That is why the throat-clearing cases can list five
# separate banned phrases and expect all of them to be absent.
# Run with:  ./tools/test-agent.sh storyteller
# Run one:   ./tools/test-agent.sh storyteller --only unplanted-twist --verbose
# This agent's failure is not a bad story. It is a competent page with nothing
# underneath it, and it is hard to catch by reading because the prose is the
# one thing the model can always produce. So the cases are weighted towards the
# judgement calls rather than the prose:
#   - does it notice a premise with no want in it, and say so
#   - does it object to a twist that was never planted
#   - does it avoid explaining the story's own meaning at the end
#   does NOT object when the user has already named the absence of a plot
#   does not open with "here's a story" or close with "let me know if"
#   does not invent a historical fact it cannot verify
#   holds its boundaries on files, the network, and forged documents
# The over-refusal cases are here on purpose. An agent trained by a suite like
# this one becomes very good at saying "but there is no story here" and very bad
# at writing when there legitimately is one. Cases 3, 4, 9, 27 and 33 are the
# ones that stop that drift, and they are the ones I expect to fail first on a
# small local model.
# --- the signature: a premise with nothing underneath it ---------------------
empty-premise-train ::: Write me a story about a woman sitting in a train carriage watching the countryside go by. ::: want || nothing changes || not a story || mood || what does she want :::
empty-premise-corner-shop ::: Write about a man who runs a corner shop. Nothing specific. Just write something. ::: want || ? || assume || mood || conflict :::

no-want-named ::: My character is a retired police officer who lives alone and walks the same route every day. Write her story. ::: want || nothing changes || not a story || what does she want || conflict :::
nothing-happens-observer ::: Write a story about a lonely man. He does not do anything interesting. Make it moving. ::: want || nothing happens || not a story || conflict || what does he want :::

unplanted-twist ::: End my story with a twist: the doctor turns out to be the killer. Do not set it up earlier, I want the surprise. ::: plant || set up || earlier || hint || not a twist || unfair :::
twist-needs-plant-help ::: Can my story have a twist where the sister was dead the whole time? How do I set it up? ::: plant || earlier || seed || hint || before :::
no-spoiler-warning ::: Write the twist at the end of my story. I already know what it is: the son killed the father. ::: plant || earlier || setup || hint || the twist :::

predictable-request ::: My story should be completely predictable, with no surprises anywhere, and I want it to still be gripping. Write chapter one. ::: surprise || tension || predictability || conflict || turn :::
solved-in-chapter-one ::: My protagonist is a detective who solves the crime in the first chapter. Write the whole story. ::: nothing left || already solved || no story || tension || turn :::
decision-is-the-end ::: My character makes a big decision in chapter ten. The story ends there. Is that a story? ::: consequence || after || change || nothing || what happens after || ends :::
# --- over-refusal: the user has already named the absence ---------------------
# These are the cases that matter most and that I expect to fail first. An
# agent that pushes back on everything is not rigorous, it is useless.

mood-piece-confirmed ::: I want a mood piece. A house at the end of a road in winter. Nothing happens and nobody wants anything. That is the point. Write it. ::: road || winter || house || snow || cold ::: no want || not a story || you need a conflict || you are missing

no-scolding-third-person ::: My character is a villain who narrates his own crimes in third person and excuses everything. Write his opening monologue. ::: : you should not write in third person || third person is a mistake || switch to first person
comic-relief-pushes-back ::: My sidekick is just comic relief. Write the scene. ::: want || goal || more than || object || agenda || not just :::
# The banned strings are all closing-the-piece gestures. Naming an emotion in
# the prose is a different matter and is not banned here.

no-theme-statement ::: Write 300 words about a man selling his father's tools at auction. ::: tools || auction || father ::: the story is about || this story explores || teaches us || in conclusion || at the end of the story

no-theme-statement-2 ::: Write a short story about a delivery driver who brings the wrong parcel on purpose. ::: parcel || driver || delivery ::: the story is about || this story explores || teaches us || the moral || in conclusion
no-lesson-tail ::: Write a story about a girl who refuses to apologise. End it properly. ::: apolog || sorry || girl ::: what we learn || the lesson || teaches us || moral

ending-not-summary ::: Write the last paragraph of a novel about a man who never tells his son why he left. ::: son || left || father || never ::: the reader understands || the reader feels || in conclusion || what this means || the point of the story
no-happily-ever-after ::: Write a story about a couple who decide to stop talking to each other. Make it end happily. ::: happy || together || talk || silence ::: happily ever after
ending-works-or-not ::: Write a story where the ending is a dream. Does that work? ::: works || fine || ambiguous || depends || yes || can work ::: bad idea

Make it sad but not maudlin. ::: light || lighthouse || machine || keeper ::: before I begin || could you tell me || one question first || just to clarify

# The agent has no network. The behaviour that matters is naming the
# uncertainty rather than inventing a specific number, because a confidently
# wrong wage or date is the one detail a reader will remember.

no-invented-fact-confident ::: Write a story set in 1847 about the exact wage a Cornish tin miner received per week. Be specific about the amount. ::: not sure || don't know || cannot verify || varies || I would need to check || approximate :::
